title: Non-healing ulcer on the lateral tongue
stem:
A 58-year-old taxi driver attends your general dental practice for a routine examination. While updating his history he mentions a "sore patch" on the left side of his tongue that has been there for **about four weeks**. It is only mildly uncomfortable and he assumed he had bitten it.

He smokes **20 cigarettes a day (roughly 35 pack-years)** and drinks **around 25 units of alcohol per week**, mostly spirits. He last saw a dentist two years ago.

On examination there is a **1.5 cm ulcer on the left lateral border of the tongue** with a rolled, indurated margin and a speckled red-and-white base. It is firm on palpation. You also palpate a **single enlarged, non-tender lymph node in the left submandibular region**. The rest of the mucosa appears normal. His lower left second molar has a fractured, sharp lingual cusp adjacent to the ulcer.

domains.name: Information gathering, assimilation & diagnosis
domains.model_answer:
My headline concern is that this is **oral squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise** — a persistent ulcer of more than three weeks in a high-risk patient at a high-risk site — so my information gathering is aimed at building the referral, not delaying it.

**History**, because the risk profile drives urgency: exact duration and any change in size; pain, referred otalgia, dysphagia, altered speech; weight loss or night sweats, because these suggest advanced disease; full smoking and alcohol quantification, because they are synergistic risk factors; previous head and neck lesions or radiotherapy; and a social history, because a taxi driver who smokes in the car may underestimate his exposure and his support network matters for what comes next.

**Examination**, because I need to document a baseline: site, size, margin character and induration of the ulcer, measured and ideally photographed with consent; full systematic soft-tissue examination of all mucosal surfaces, because field change means synchronous lesions are possible; and a structured neck examination of all lymph node levels, recording size, consistency, tenderness and fixation — a firm, non-tender, enlarged node is worrying for metastasis rather than infection.

I would note the fractured cusp as a possible traumatic cause, but I would **not** let it falsely reassure me. The classic trap is to smooth the tooth and review for two weeks — trauma may coexist with cancer, and the rolled indurated margin, the speckled base, the site, and the node all point away from a simple traumatic ulcer.

**Differential diagnosis**: oral squamous cell carcinoma (my working diagnosis); traumatic ulcer from the fractured cusp; major aphthous ulcer; less likely, a deep fungal or granulomatous ulcer such as TB, or a chronic hyperplastic candidosis on a background of erythroleukoplakia.

**Investigations**: definitive diagnosis is by incisional biopsy, but that belongs in secondary care — in practice my investigation is the urgent referral itself. I would not order radiographs for the ulcer, because imaging for staging (MRI, ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration of the node) is a secondary-care decision, and any exposure I take must be justified under IRMER 2017.

domains.name: Management of scenario
domains.model_answer:
Today my priority is to get this man onto the **urgent suspected-cancer pathway** — in England that is the two-week-wait referral under **NICE NG12**, which specifically includes unexplained oral ulceration lasting more than three weeks, and a persistent unexplained neck lump.

So today I would:

1. **Refer urgently** to oral and maxillofacial surgery / head and neck oncology on the local suspected-cancer proforma, the same day, marked as a two-week-wait referral — including my clinical findings, a photograph if I have one, the risk factors, and the node, because a complete referral avoids triage delay.
2. **Tell the patient honestly but proportionately**: I would explain that the patch has features that need a specialist to look at urgently, that one of the things they will rule out is cancer, and that being seen within two weeks is the system working, not a cause for panic. Honesty here is a *Montgomery* and GDC Standards issue — he cannot engage with an urgent appointment he does not understand the importance of.
3. **Smooth or dress the fractured cusp** so it is not traumatising the area — because removing the traumatic element helps the specialist interpret the lesion — but I would document clearly that this is symptomatic care alongside referral, **not** a substitute for it.
4. **Offer very brief smoking and alcohol advice** and record it, because cessation improves every outcome from here, but today is not the day for a long lecture.

Red flags I am acting on: ulcer >3 weeks, induration, rolled margin, speckled erythroleukoplakic base, high-risk site, high-risk patient, and a suspicious node. Any one of these justifies urgent referral; he has all of them.

What I would **not** do: prescribe antibiotics or antifungals "to see if it settles", or arrange a two-week review as the primary plan — watchful waiting in this picture is the single biggest cause of avoidable delay in oral cancer diagnosis.

domains.name: Management planning & execution
domains.model_answer:
My plan runs in three phases: **stabilise, definitive, maintenance** — with the definitive phase led by secondary care.

**Stabilise (this week, my responsibility):** the urgent referral is sent and receipt confirmed; the sharp cusp is smoothed; simple analgesia and a benzydamine mouthwash for comfort if he needs it [verify against current BNF/SDCEP]; and I make sure he has the referral details in writing with a contact number.

**Definitive (secondary care, but I should be able to describe it):** the head and neck team will typically examine, photograph and biopsy the lesion, image with MRI of the primary site and ultrasound ± fine-needle aspiration of the node, stage the disease via the multidisciplinary team, and treat with surgery ± radiotherapy depending on stage. My role is to have sent a referral good enough that none of that is delayed.

**My dental contribution before treatment:** if he is diagnosed and heading for radiotherapy, he will need an urgent **pre-radiotherapy dental assessment** — teeth of poor prognosis in the field are usually removed beforehand, because extractions after radiotherapy carry a risk of osteoradionecrosis. So I would get his mouth as stable as I can quickly: caries control, extraction of hopeless teeth if the oncology team's timeline allows, fluoride (2,800 ppm or 5,000 ppm toothpaste [verify against current BNF/SDCEP]) and preventive advice per *Delivering Better Oral Health*.

**Maintenance:** whatever the outcome, he becomes a high-risk recall patient — short recall intervals under the NICE dental recall guideline, lifelong soft-tissue surveillance because field change means a second primary is a real risk, ongoing smoking and alcohol support, and high-fluoride prevention if he ends up with radiotherapy-induced xerostomia.

**Options including doing nothing:** doing nothing, or reviewing informally, risks progression from a potentially curable T1 lesion to advanced disease — I would explain that the option exists but that I strongly advise against it, and if he declined referral I would document that discussion in detail and keep the door open at every contact.

domains.name: Professionalism, ethics & medicolegal
domains.model_answer:
**Consent and honesty:** under *Montgomery* and GDC *Standards* (principle 1, putting patients' interests first, and 2.3, giving patients the information they need in a way they understand), he needs to know why the referral is urgent. I would use the word "cancer" as a possibility being excluded, because vague language ("just a specialist check") is a known cause of patients not attending two-week-wait appointments. Consent for today's referral, the photograph, and the cusp adjustment are all recorded.

**Documentation:** contemporaneous notes with the lesion's site, size, appearance and induration, ideally a photograph, the node findings, the risk-factor history, the exact advice given, the referral date, pathway and where it was sent, and the safety-netting instructions. If he ever alleges delayed diagnosis, the record is my defence — and more importantly it is what lets the next clinician pick the case up seamlessly.

**Safety-netting, said out loud:** "If the appointment doesn't arrive within two weeks, contact us straight away — don't wait. If the ulcer bleeds, grows quickly, or you have trouble swallowing, seek urgent care." I would also diarise a practice-side check that the appointment actually happened, because referral systems fail and the duty of care doesn't end at the send button.

**If he refuses referral:** he has capacity, so he can refuse — but refusal must be informed. I would explore his reasons (fear, work pressure as a self-employed driver, cost of time off), give the information in unambiguous terms including that early oral cancer is very treatable and late oral cancer is not, document the discussion verbatim where possible, inform his GP with his consent, and re-raise it at every contact. I cannot compel him, but I must be able to show he refused *knowing* what he was refusing.

**Referral threshold and my limits:** this is over my referral threshold by a wide margin, and I would say so plainly: diagnosis and management of a suspected oral malignancy is beyond primary dental care, and beyond this point I would be guided by the head and neck team.

marks_lost: Attributing the ulcer to the fractured cusp and arranging "smooth and review in 2 weeks" as the primary plan — the classic delayed-diagnosis trap.
Saying "refer" without specifying the pathway (urgent / two-week-wait / NICE NG12) or what makes the referral urgent.
Omitting the neck examination, or finding the node and not connecting it to the working diagnosis.
Not quantifying smoking and alcohol, or forgetting they are synergistic risk factors.
Being vague or evasive with the patient about why the referral is urgent — examiners want the honesty conversation handled explicitly.
No safety-netting for the referral itself (what happens if the appointment doesn't arrive).
Forgetting the dentist's ongoing role: pre-radiotherapy dental assessment, fluoride, lifelong surveillance.

probes.q: The patient says he can't afford time off work and asks you to just keep an eye on it. What do you say?
probes.a: I'd acknowledge the real pressure he's under, then be direct: the features of this patch mean it could be a cancer, early treatment is far shorter and more successful than late treatment, and delaying could ultimately cost him far more work time. I'd explore practical fixes — appointment timing, a letter for work — and if he still refuses, document the informed refusal in detail, inform his GP with consent, and actively re-raise it rather than passively 'keeping an eye on it'.

probes.q: Why not take a biopsy yourself in practice?
probes.a: Because with a lesion this suspicious, an incisional biopsy in primary care can delay rather than speed things up: the two-week-wait pathway will re-biopsy to their own protocol, a poorly sited biopsy can make definitive assessment harder, and a negative result from a small sample could falsely reassure. NICE NG12 and local pathways expect referral on clinical suspicion, not proof.

probes.q: What examination findings specifically distinguish a traumatic ulcer from a malignant one?
probes.a: A traumatic ulcer is usually soft, tender, has flat non-indurated margins, an obvious matching cause, and heals within two weeks of removing that cause. Malignancy is suggested by induration, a rolled everted margin, a granular or speckled base, relative painlessness, persistence beyond three weeks despite removing trauma, and associated firm cervical lymphadenopathy.

probes.q: He is later booked for radiotherapy. What is your role now?
probes.a: Urgent pre-radiotherapy dental assessment coordinated with the oncology team's timeline: remove teeth of hopeless or poor prognosis in the radiation field beforehand because post-radiotherapy extractions risk osteoradionecrosis; stabilise caries; start high-fluoride toothpaste and prevention per Delivering Better Oral Health; plan for xerostomia; and set up short-interval lifelong recall for a second primary.

references: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (head and neck section)
GDC Standards for the Dental Team — principles 1 and 2
Delivering Better Oral Health (OHID) — fluoride and cessation advice
RCS / BAOMS guidance on oral cancer referral and pre-radiotherapy dental care
